title: Stocks
intro: A stock, or share, is a slice of ownership in a company. Owning it gives you a claim on the company's future profits, a vote on some decisions, and nothing guaranteed. This page explains what that claim is worth, how it pays you, and how stocks are grouped and compared.

blocks.text: A company that has issued 1 billion shares and is worth \$50 billion has a share price of \$50; the total, $\text{price} \times \text{shares outstanding}$, is its market capitalization (market cap). Owning one share makes you a part-owner of everything the company owns, after everyone it owes has been paid. That makes shareholders the residual claimants: last in line if the company fails, but entitled to all the upside if it thrives. That position is why stocks have higher expected returns than bonds of the same company, and why they can fall to zero.

Shareholders have limited liability: you can lose what you paid, not more (unless you bought with borrowed money). They usually get one vote per share to elect the board of directors, which hires and oversees management.

A stock's return comes from two places: dividends, cash paid out of profits, and price change. Over the long run price change reflects growth in the company's earnings and changes in how much investors are willing to pay for each dollar of earnings (the valuation multiple). For the S&P 500 over the last century, dividends supplied roughly 40% of total return; since the 1990s yields have been lower and buybacks have taken over part of that role.

items: Dividends: declared by the board, often quarterly in the US and semi-annually or yearly in Europe and Japan. Key dates: the ex-dividend date (buy on or after it and you don't get the next dividend; the price usually drops by about the dividend that morning) and the payment date. Dividend yield = yearly dividend / price.

Buybacks (share repurchases): the company buys its own shares, so each remaining share owns a larger slice. Economically similar to a dividend, but taxed only when you sell, and flexible. A buyback at a high price destroys value just as a bad acquisition does.
Payout ratio: dividends / earnings. A ratio over 100% for long is a warning that the dividend may be cut.
Dividend reinvestment (a DRIP) buys more shares with each dividend, compounding the holding.

blocks.text: A high dividend yield is not free money. The price falls by the dividend on the ex-date, so a dividend is a transfer from the share price to your pocket, and in taxable accounts it is taxed. A very high yield is often a sign the market expects a cut.
Stock splits, share classes and preferred stock

items: Splits: a 2-for-1 split doubles the shares and halves the price. Nothing of value changes; it just makes the price per share smaller.

Share classes: some companies have several classes with different votes, so founders keep control (Alphabet's A, B and C shares, Meta's A and B). Index providers and governance-minded investors watch these closely.

Preferred stock: pays a fixed dividend that must be paid before common dividends, ranks above common stock in a bankruptcy, and usually has no vote. It behaves more like a long bond than a stock, and often has a call feature letting the company redeem it.
ADRs (American Depositary Receipts) let US investors buy foreign companies on US exchanges; the price moves with the home share and the exchange rate.

blocks.text: The long-run return on a stock market can be split into three pieces (the 'building blocks' approach used by Bogle and others):

Starting from a 2% dividend yield and 4 to 5% nominal earnings growth, you expect roughly 6 to 7% nominal a year if valuations stay put. A rising P/E adds to that for a while; a falling one subtracts. Over decades the first two terms dominate; over a few years the third does, which is why short-run returns are so hard to predict and long-run ones a little less so.

items: By size: large-cap (roughly over \$10 billion), mid-cap (\$2 to 10 billion), small-cap (\$300 million to \$2 billion), micro-cap below. Small stocks are more volatile and less liquid.

By sector: the Global Industry Classification Standard (GICS) has 11 sectors: information technology, health care, financials, consumer discretionary, consumer staples, industrials, energy, materials, utilities, real estate and communication services.
Cyclical and defensive: cyclicals (autos, materials, industrials, luxury goods) rise and fall with the economy; defensives (utilities, staples, health care) sell things people buy anyway.

Growth and value: growth stocks have high expected earnings growth and high valuations; value stocks are cheap against their earnings, book value or cash flow. Historically value has earned a premium over long periods, though with long droughts such as 2007 to 2020.
By region: US, developed ex-US (Europe, Japan, Australia, Canada), and emerging markets (China, India, Taiwan, Brazil and others), which add growth, political and currency risk.
Earnings reports: public companies report every quarter in the US (half-yearly in much of Europe). Prices move on results against expectations, not on whether the results are good in absolute terms.
Issuing new shares dilutes existing owners: the same profits are split among more shares. Stock-based pay to employees does the same slowly; watch the growth in the share count.
Mergers and acquisitions: the target's shares usually jump toward the offer price; the buyer's often fall, as acquirers tend to overpay on average.
Spin-offs: a company separates a division into a new listed company and hands its shares to existing owners.
Bankruptcy: in a US Chapter 11 reorganization the old shares are usually wiped out and the creditors become the new owners.

blocks.title: Market cap
blocks.text: A company has 400 million shares at \$75. What is its market cap? If it buys back 20 million shares at that price with cash, what happens to its market cap and to each remaining share's slice of the company?
solution: The buyback spends \$1.5 billion of cash, so the company (and its market cap, other things equal) is worth \$28.5 billion, split over 380 million shares: still \$75 each. Each share now owns $1/380\text{ m}$ of the company instead of $1/400\text{ m}$, about 5.3% more of the remaining business. A buyback at a fair price neither creates nor destroys value; it helps remaining owners only if the shares were cheap.

blocks.title: Building-block return
blocks.text: A market has a dividend yield of 1.5%, you expect earnings to grow 5% a year, and you think its P/E will drift from 24 down to 20 over the next 10 years. Roughly what yearly return do you expect?
blocks.hint: Turn the P/E change into a yearly rate with a tenth root.

blocks.title: The ex-dividend drop
blocks.text: A stock trades at \$40 the day before it goes ex-dividend on a \$0.50 dividend. Ignoring other news, where should it open, and are you better off buying before or after?
solution: It should open at about \$39.50. Buying before gets you \$0.50 of cash and a \$39.50 share; buying after gets you a \$39.50 share. You are no richer either way, and in a taxable account the dividend may be taxed, so buying just to 'capture' the dividend usually makes you slightly poorer.
